script:
This robot learned to walk in a world that doesn't exist.
Researchers at ETH Zurich trained a four-legged robot inside a physics simulator.
The crazy part: they ran thousands of virtual copies at once on one GPU.
Each one trips, falls, resets, and tries again.
Steps that follow the commanded speed earn points.
Flat ground took under four minutes. Uneven ground took about twenty.
Then the trained brain went into the real robot, and it walked.
The wildest part is what the simulator gets wrong.
Friction is a guess, motors lag, and foot contact is really hard to model.
So the engineers make the fake world messy on purpose.
Every virtual robot gets different friction and random shoves.
Reality just looks like one more version it already practiced.
Grabbing things is still harder, because touching objects is where simulations break down.
Robots now get their basic moves in a virtual gym before they touch the real ground.
In a few years, I think every new humanoid will learn to walk this way first. Follow for more tech, AI and robotics stories.

sources.supports: Trained the quadrupedal ANYmal robot with Isaac Gym on a single workstation GPU using thousands of simulated robots in parallel; ETH Zurich affiliation; flat terrain policies in under four minutes and uneven terrain in twenty minutes; policy transferred to the real robot; robots reset when they fall; reward encourages following commanded velocities; friction randomized per robot and pushes applied during episodes.

Full paper text: thousands of robots simulated in parallel on the GPU; friction sampled per robot in a range of 0.5 to 1.25; random pushes to the base during episodes; robots reset when they fall; reward terms reward following commanded velocities.

Humanoid RL walking trained by trial and error in simulation with thousands of virtual robots, each with unique physical parameters; domain randomization used to bridge the sim-to-real gap; policies transferred to the real robot without tuning.

Sim-to-real defined as training in a physics engine and running the result on hardware; the sim-to-real gap comes from approximated friction, hard-to-model contact, motor delay and noisy sensors; locomotion transfers well because gravity, ground reaction and momentum are well modeled, while manipulation transfers badly because it is contact-heavy; grasping is still largely learned from teleoperation on real hardware.
